idiom_name: frozen flags object parsed from process.env; OpenFeature server SDK when flags are managed
implementation_notes: The router collapses into a small module: process.env is parsed once at start-up into a frozen flags object (or a Map), and the toggle point is a plain property read. Inject the flags object instead of reading process.env inside functions, so tests can pass {newCheckout: true} and neither branch needs the environment to be manipulated. When flags are administered centrally, the OpenFeature server SDK replaces the hand-written router with a vendor-neutral evaluation API - OpenFeature.setProvider(...) plus client.getBooleanValue(key, default, context) - which is the point where targeting, cohorts and an audit trail become available. The classic router object is still justified when the decision depends on request context; a bare module-level constant is not, because it freezes the flag at import time.
pitfalls: process.env values are strings, so 'false' is truthy: always compare with 'true' instead of testing the value in a condition.

A module-level flags object is evaluated once at import; a runtime flip needs an accessor, a provider or an explicit reload, otherwise the constant keeps the start-up value for the life of the process.
Bundlers substitute process.env expressions at build time for browser code, silently converting a runtime toggle into a build-time one.
Long-lived Node processes share one flag value across requests, so per-user targeting cannot be implemented by mutating it.
